name: sol_heuristics_17
description: Rounding/fee inconsistency exploitable by splitting a financial operation into many small calls
question: The source file in `source` implements a function performing a financial computation (e.g., deposit, mint, withdraw, fee or interest calculation) that involves integer division or per-call rounding/truncation, such that invoking it repeatedly with smaller amounts yields a materially different, more favorable-to-caller cumulative state than invoking it once with the aggregate amount, and this rounding-driven discrepancy is neither bounded, documented as intentional/negligible dust, nor guarded against (e.g., no minimum-amount check or rounding-direction safeguard), excluding cases where the difference is provably negligible or explicitly accepted as safe by design.
criteria: deposit() computes shares = amount * totalShares / totalAssets separately per call with truncation, letting a user accumulate more shares by splitting one large deposit into many small deposits

calculateFee() computes fee = amount * feeBps / 10000 using integer division per call, so splitting a transfer into many small transfers rounds the fee down to zero each time and avoids the fee owed on the aggregate amount
withdraw() rounds down the deducted balance per call, so repeated small withdrawals leave a larger uncollected remainder than a single withdrawal of the same aggregate amount

interest accrual function computes interest = principal * rate / PRECISION per call and resets/truncates state between calls, causing repeated small accrual calls to produce less total interest than one call over the combined period

swap() or mint() applies a rounding-in-favor-of-user step independently on each call, allowing an attacker to repeatedly call with minimal amounts to extract more output tokens than a single call with the summed input would yield
